There is a specific kind of quiet that only exists at 6 a.m. on a weekday, before the world has remembered it is supposed to be busy.

I have always loved that hour. Not enough to be disciplined about waking up for it, but enough to feel a small, private triumph on the days I do. The light is different then — it hasn't made up its mind yet. It is not the golden, performative light of sunset, which knows it is beautiful and wants to be photographed. Morning light is provisional, pale and blue at the edges, as if it is asking permission to enter the room. The coffee maker gurgles with more sincerity than at any other time of day. The emails have not yet started arriving. For a few minutes, you can pretend that time is not a conveyor belt but a wide, still lake, and you are just floating.

I think a lot about time, maybe because I never feel like I have the right relationship to it. When I was a child, summer lasted forever. I mean that literally — I can still viscerally recall the endlessness of a July afternoon when I was nine. An hour was a continent. You could leave the house after breakfast, build a fort, renegotiate its treaty of ownership three times, become bored, become inspired again, and return home for lunch only to discover that it was 11:47 a.m. Now, embarrassingly, I will put a bagel in the toaster and check my phone while I wait, and somehow lose twenty minutes and resurface with a vague anxiety that I have forgotten to do something important.

Somewhere along the line, we trade duration for density. Adult years are short but packed. Every day is layered with overlapping contexts — you are an employee, a partner, a friend, a child, a person trying to drink enough water — and all those layers compress time like sediment into rock. And maybe that's why we become so nostalgic. Not because the past was better, but because the past was spacious.

One of my favorite human inventions for fighting this compression is the library.

Not just libraries as buildings, though I love the buildings themselves — the older ones with their brass lamps and card catalogs that are now just decorative, as well as the newer, brighter ones that look like community living rooms. I mean the idea of the library. The operating principle that some things should be available to everyone, without need for justification, and that one of those things should be stories.

A library is a quiet rebellion against the logic that everything must be earned, optimized, or monetized. You walk in and a person at a desk will help you find whatever you want to know, for free, with no ulterior motive beyond a genuine belief that you should know it. You can sit there for hours and no one will ask you to buy anything. In a world that feels increasingly like an airport terminal mall — every surface an advertisement, every moment an opportunity to upsell you — a library is a sanctuary where you are not a consumer. You are a patron. An old word that actually means something like “a person under protection.”

And the books themselves. Millions of them, holding completely contradictory ideas, all housed politely next to each other. A manual on beekeeping next to a memoir about grief next to a graphic novel about teenage robots next to a 14th-century Persian poem. No algorithm has decided you should only see the beekeeping book because you once clicked on honey. It's all there, indifferent to your preferences, waiting to be stumbled upon. I believe serendipity is a muscle and libraries are its gym.

Of course, we now have the internet, which is often described as the world’s largest library. But it doesn’t feel that way to me. The internet is the world’s largest flea market and performance stage and surveillance apparatus and argument. It has all the information of a library, but none of the ethos. A library preserves. The internet agitates. A library says, “Here you are safe to be curious in private.” The internet says, “Here you will be curious in public, and we will keep score.” I love the internet too, in the way you can love a brilliant, chaotic friend who always gets you into trouble. But I wouldn’t want to live inside it.

Maybe what I’m really circling around is attention. Because that’s the other thing that has changed — not just time, but what we do with it.

Attention used to be something you paid, like a toll you chose to hand over. Now it feels more like something that is mined from you while you’re not looking, and then sold. Every app, every platform, every news cycle is designed by thousands of very smart people whose job is to keep you looking just a little longer. It works. It works on everyone. I have felt my own brain become twitchier over the last ten years, more prone to reaching for the phone during the two-minute microwave wait, as if stillness itself has become mildly intolerable.

And so I have been trying, in small, unsystematic ways, to re-train myself. Not in a grand digital detox, go-live-in-a-cabin way. I don’t want to become a person who brags about not owning a television. I just want to be able to read a book for an hour without checking anything. I want to be able to stand in line at the grocery store and just stand in line, looking at the strange universe of gum flavors, letting my mind wander into its own weird corners instead of immediately outsourcing my consciousness to a feed.

The most effective method I’ve found is embarrassingly simple: I carry a small paperback with me everywhere. Not a Kindle, not a phone, but an actual physical book that will get bent in my pocket. When I feel the itch to scroll, I read a page instead. Sometimes I only read a paragraph before I’m interrupted, but that paragraph does something different to my brain. A social media post is designed to make you want the next post. A paragraph in a good novel is designed to make you dwell inside it. One creates hunger; the other creates fullness.

There’s a scene I keep coming back to from a novel I read years ago — I can’t even remember the title now, which is perhaps part of its power, that it has dissolved into my own thinking. A character, an old astronomer, is explaining to a child why he likes looking at stars that have already died. The light we see from some stars, he says, left them millions of years ago. By the time it reaches us, the star itself is gone. But the light is still on its way. It is still beautiful, still true on arrival. The child asks if that isn’t sad, and the astronomer says no, it’s the opposite of sad. It means the universe remembers.

I think about that whenever I feel pressure to be current, relevant, on top of things. The astronomer’s view gives us permission to be late. Some light takes a long time to get here. Some books wait on the shelf for twenty years for the right reader. Some ideas you had as a teenager turn out to be good, but you need a decade of living to have the skill to execute them. We are told constantly to hurry — to publish, to post, to pitch, to not miss our moment. But perhaps our moment is not a moment at all, but a slow transit.

I don’t really know where I’m going with all this. That’s part of the point of writing freely — you are allowed to not have a thesis. In school, we were taught that every essay needs an argument, a neat conclusion that ties everything together with a bow. Real thought doesn’t work like that. Real thought meanders. It notices a pigeon on the windowsill in the middle of contemplating mortality and follows the pigeon for a while, because the pigeon is there and it is interesting that it has iridescent feathers on its neck.

If I had to find a thread, though, it would be this: I think we get the world wrong when we try to make it too efficient. We want faster communication, faster food, faster shipping, faster enlightenment. But the parts of life that actually make us feel alive are almost defiantly inefficient. Friendship is inefficient. It requires hours of loitering with no agenda. Reading a 400-page novel is inefficient when you could read a summary. Learning to play the guitar badly is inefficient when you could just listen to someone else play it perfectly. Sleep is wildly inefficient — you spend a third of your life unconscious and drooling. Love is perhaps the most inefficient project of all, requiring staggering amounts of time, misunderstanding, forgiveness, and leftover takeout containers.

And yet.

And yet when we look back on our lives, it will not be the efficient moments we cherish. No one on their deathbed wishes they had unsubscribed from newsletters more quickly. We will remember the long afternoons, the conversations that went on until 2 a.m., the books we read twice, the walks with no destination, the people we waited for, and who waited for us.

There is a courage in allowing things to take their time. A quiet courage. The kind that doesn’t win awards but makes life feel less like an emergency.

So if I could wish one small thing for whoever is reading this — which will be you, in your own particular quiet hour, your own provisional light — it would be this: Take five minutes today and do one thing inefficiently on purpose. Make tea with loose leaves. Write a letter by hand. Walk without headphones. Sit on a bench and watch how the trees move when they think no one is watching. Let a little dead starlight finally land.

It has been traveling a long way just to get to you.
